verses.verse:
न्यूनाधिक्येन कालस्य वाक्यार्थः परिवर्त्यते।
ताल काल प्रभावेन राग भावो विशिष्यते।१३१।
verses.text: By lessening or lengthening time, the meaning of a sentence is changed; by the power of tāla and time, the feeling of a rāga is made distinct.

commentary.text: That is, in the world of music, for the expression of feeling, laya (tempo) and tāla (metric cycle) have an important place along with rāga. Just as various chandas (metres) are described in the world of literature, so many kinds of tāla are described in music. If the number of mātrās (beats) and a particular order of short and long [syllables] give birth to a metre, then the number of mātrās and a particular division of the mātrās create a tāla.

This is why Tāla Dhamār, Tāla Dīpcandī and Āḍā Cārtāl, though all are tālas of the same number of mātrās (beats), have their own separate existence because of differences in the division of the mātrās. To know clearly the importance of tāla in rāga, a few sentences are offered. For example: (1) roko mat, jāne do [don't stop (him), let (him) go]. roko, mat jāne do [stop (him), don't let (him) go]. (2) jā, pānī lā [go, bring water]. jāpānī lā [bring the Japanese one]. (3) surāhī banā [make a water-jar]. surā hī banā [make only liquor]. su rāhī banā [become a good traveller]. In these sentences time is the cause of the change of meaning; so it is easy to understand and to explain the sense of tāla on the basis of words. In stringed instruments (tantu vādya), the responsibility of making clear the sense of tāla and laya (tempo) is given to the right hand. For it is said (śrutir mātā layaḥ pitā - śruti is the mother, laya the father) (the mother's place being on the left side and the father's on the right is also a symbol of Indian tradition.) But in wind instruments (suṣira vādya) like the bansī (bamboo flute), both hands are taken up by the notes alone. So the tongue alone has to represent laya, tāla and words. Sitar players make many words from dā and rā, e.g. - dā dir dā rā, dir dā dir dā, dā radā –ra dā. In the same way bansī players imagine various words from ṭa and ka, e.g. - ṭā ṭak ṭā kā, ṭakṭak ṭā kā ṭā kaṭā –ka ṭā, and so on; with such rhythm-showing words they can follow the sitar. If one wishes to translate these symbolic words into meaningful words, a special vocabulary can be formed, e.g. -

commentary.text: In the same way other words too can be translated into the language of instruments. This proves that it must have been metrical poetry of regular timing that gave birth to the tālas. From here it became necessary to show the meeting of literature and music. Sādhakas (learners) should try to count some poems by their mātrās and to write and recite them with the proper tāla. Then they should try to blend them with a rāga; only then will they understand bandiśes (compositions) properly. Although in old texts you will find many bandiśes in which the mātrās of short and long syllables are not kept as they are - in some places a short syllable takes even more mātrās than a long one, and elsewhere a long syllable is given even less time than a short one - such bandiśes can confuse learners. So they should treat those bandiśes as exceptions, and at the beginning, not considering themselves fit for them, attend only to simple bandiśes. Then, gradually becoming able, they will come to know the secret of those bandiśes too. Just as nourishing food is harmful for a patient, so for those of little knowledge a deep subject does not increase knowledge but increases pride. If the grace of the guru (teacher) is not obtained, that same śāstra, instead of making me a sādhaka, can present me as a bādhaka (hindrance). So my one invaluable suggestion for sādhakas is this:
